pairs.source_text: Post quos Sex. Marius Hispaniarum ditissimus defertur incestasse filiam et saxo Tarpeio deicitur.
pairs.question: Quis, Hispaniarum ditissimus, sub Tiberio incesti accusatus saxo Tarpeio deiectus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Who, the richest man of the Spanish provinces, was accused of incest under Tiberius and thrown from the Tarpeian Rock, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Sextus Marius + the Spanish provinces + the Tarpeian Rock; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Sex. Marius Hispaniarum ditissimus ... saxo Tarpeio deicitur'. Closed-book: Sextus Marius, the richest man in Spain whose gold/copper mines Tiberius then confiscated, is a memorable Tacitean vignette of the terror.

pairs.source_text: Non omiserim praesagium Tiberii de Servio Galba tum consule; quem accitum et diversis sermonibus pertemptatum postremo Graecis verbis in hanc sententiam adlocutus 'et tu, Galba, quandoque degustabis imperium,' seram ac brevem potentiam significans
pairs.question: De quo viro, tum consule, Tiberius praedixit eum quandoque imperium degustaturum esse, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Concerning what man, then consul, did Tiberius foretell that he would one day taste of empire, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Tiberius + Servius Galba; single named person, supported verbatim by 'praesagium Tiberii de Servio Galba ... et tu, Galba, quandoque degustabis imperium'. Closed-book: Tiberius's prophecy of Galba's brief future reign (Galba did become emperor in 68-69) is a famous anecdote.

pairs.source_text: scientia Chaldaeorum artis, cuius apiscendae otium apud Rhodum, magistrum Thrasullum habuit
pairs.question: Quem magistrum artis Chaldaeorum Tiberius apud Rhodum habuit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Whom did Tiberius have as his teacher of the Chaldaean (astrological) art at Rhodes, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Tiberius + Rhodes + the Chaldaean art; single named person, supported verbatim by 'apud Rhodum, magistrum Thrasullum habuit' (text spells it 'Thrasullum'). Closed-book: Thrasyllus, the astrologer who taught Tiberius on Rhodes, is a stock figure of the reign.

pairs.source_text: cum de Agrippina auditum, quam interfecto Seiano spe sustentatam provixisse reor, et postquam nihil de saevitia remittebatur, voluntate extinctam, nisi si negatis alimentis adsimulatus est finis qui videretur sponte sumptus.
pairs.question: Quo mortis genere Agrippina, Germanici uxor et Tiberii nurus, vitam finivit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: By what kind of death did Agrippina, wife of Germanicus and daughter-in-law of Tiberius, end her life, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Agrippina the Elder (wife of Germanicus, Tiberius's daughter-in-law) to distinguish her from the younger Agrippina; the death by starvation is supported by 'voluntate extinctam' and 'negatis alimentis ... sponte sumptus'. Closed-book: the elder Agrippina's death by self-starvation under Tiberius is a stock fact of the reign.

pairs.source_text: Paulo Fabio L. Vitellio consulibus post longum saeculorum ambitum avis phoenix in Aegyptum venit praebuitque materiem doctissimis indigenarum et Graecorum multa super eo miraculo disserendi.
pairs.question: In quam terram avem phoenicem post longum saeculorum ambitum advenisse Tacitus refert?
pairs.question_en: Into what land does Tacitus report that the phoenix bird came after a long cycle of ages?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the phoenix + Egypt; single place, supported verbatim by 'avis phoenix in Aegyptum venit'. Closed-book: the appearance of the phoenix in Egypt is the famous core of Tacitus's ethnographic phoenix excursus. One crisp fact kept from the digression.

pairs.source_text: neque enim multo post supremi Tiberio consules, Cn. Acerronius C. Pontius, magistratum occepere
pairs.question: Qui consules sub Tiberio supremi magistratum inierunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which consuls were the last to enter office under Tiberius, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Tiberius + the consulship; two named persons, supported verbatim by 'supremi Tiberio consules, Cn. Acerronius C. Pontius, magistratum occepere'. Closed-book, verifiable: these were the ordinary consuls of AD 37, the last under Tiberius.

pairs.source_text: mutatisque saepius locis tandem apud promunturium Miseni consedit in villa cui L. Lucullus quondam dominus.
pairs.question: Apud quod promunturium Tiberius, in villa quondam L. Luculli, vitam finivit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: At what promontory did Tiberius end his life, in the villa that had once belonged to Lucius Lucullus, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Tiberius + the villa of Lucullus; single place, supported verbatim by 'apud promunturium Miseni consedit in villa cui L. Lucullus quondam dominus'. Closed-book: Tiberius's death at Misenum, in the former villa of Lucullus, is among the best-known facts of his end.

pairs.source_text: sic Tiberius finivit octavo et septuagesimo aetatis anno.
pairs.question: Quoto aetatis anno Tiberius vitam finivit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: In what year of his age did Tiberius end his life, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Tiberius; single number, supported verbatim by 'finivit octavo et septuagesimo aetatis anno'. Closed-book number fact: Tiberius died in his 78th year (AD 37).

pairs.source_text: septimum decimum kal. Aprilis interclusa anima creditus est mortalitatem explevisse
pairs.question: Quo die Tiberius, interclusa anima, mortalitatem explevisse creditus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: On what day was Tiberius, his breath cut off, believed to have died, per Tacitus?
pairs.answer_en: On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April (16 March).
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Tiberius + a date; single date, supported verbatim by 'septimum decimum kal. Aprilis interclusa anima creditus est mortalitatem explevisse'. Closed-book: the date of Tiberius's death (a.d. XVII Kal. Apr. = 16 March, AD 37) is a fixed historical fact. Tacitus notes he was only believed dead, then revived ('creditus est').

pairs.source_text: Macro intrepidus opprimi senem iniectu multae vestis iubet discedique ab limine.
pairs.question: Quis senem Tiberium reviviscentem iniectu multae vestis opprimi iussit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Who ordered the old man Tiberius, as he revived, to be smothered by piling on a heap of clothing, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Macro + Tiberius; single named agent, supported verbatim by 'Macro intrepidus opprimi senem iniectu multae vestis iubet'. Closed-book: that Macro the praetorian prefect smothered the reviving Tiberius is a famous detail of the emperor's death.

pairs.source_text: et multo gratantum concursu ad capienda imperii primordia G. Caesar egrediebatur
pairs.question: Quis, Tiberio mortuo, ad capienda imperii primordia egressus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Who came forth to take up the beginnings of empire when Tiberius had died, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Tiberius's death + the succession; single named person, supported verbatim by 'ad capienda imperii primordia G. Caesar egrediebatur'. Closed-book: Gaius Caesar (Caligula), grandson of Tiberius and son of Germanicus, succeeded Tiberius in AD 37.

pairs.source_text: Dein Rhodo regressus vacuos principis penatis duodecim annis, mox rei Romanae arbitrium tribus ferme et viginti obtinuit.
pairs.question: Per quot fere annos Tiberius rei Romanae arbitrium obtinuit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.answer: Per tres ferme et viginti annos.
pairs.question_en: For about how many years did Tiberius hold sway over the Roman state, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Tiberius; single number, supported verbatim by 'rei Romanae arbitrium tribus ferme et viginti obtinuit'. Closed-book length-of-reign fact: Tiberius ruled about twenty-three years (AD 14-37).
